name: Door-in-the-Face Technique
description: Opening with a request expected to be refused, then retreating to the smaller request actually wanted, produces more compliance with that smaller request than asking for it directly -- read by the target as a concession worth reciprocating.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in tiered upsell/downsell flows and donation asks that open with a large suggested amount before presenting a smaller one, framed as a concession.
prevalence_note: Widely taught alongside foot-in-the-door as a named compliance technique in persuasion-design and dark-patterns discourse, though less universally cited than e.g. anchoring or scarcity.

findings.description: Making an extreme initial request that is expected to be refused, then retreating to a smaller target request, produces significantly more compliance with the smaller request than asking for it directly — across three experiments, an effect the authors attribute to a norm of reciprocal concessions (the requester's retreat is read as a concession the target should reciprocate).
findings.source_title: Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
